passages.t: Do not rejoice: the feast and the exile
passages.happening:
‘Do not rejoice, O Israel, with exultation like the nations, for you have played the harlot against your God’ (verse 1). They have made love for hire on every threshing floor. The threshing floor and the winepress will not feed them (verse 2). ‘They will not remain in the land of the LORD; Ephraim will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria’ (verse 3). Their offerings will be like the bread of mourners, which defiles all who eat it (verse 4). What will they do on the day of the LORD's feast (verse 5)? Those who flee will be gathered by Egypt and buried at Memphis, and thorns will grow over their treasures (verse 6).

‘The days of punishment have come’ (verse 7). The people call the prophet a fool and the inspired man insane, because their guilt and hostility are great. The prophet is Ephraim's watchman, but snares are set on his paths, and there is hostility even in the house of his God (verse 8). They have corrupted themselves deeply, as in the days of Gibeah, and God will remember their guilt (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The setting seems to be a harvest festival, most likely the Feast of Tabernacles in the autumn, when grain had been threshed and grapes pressed and the people celebrated with great joy. Many scholars think Hosea spoke these words in public at such a feast, perhaps at Bethel, which would explain the hostile reaction. Threshing floors were open places where grain was beaten and winnowed. They were places of celebration at harvest, and apparently also of fertility rites linked with Baal. A good harvest was often seen as a god's payment, and Hosea turns that into an accusation.

The threat of exile fits the 730s or 720s BC, after Tiglath-pileser III had already deported people from Galilee and Gilead. Outside the land there would be no altar and no way to offer firstfruits. Food in a house of mourning was unclean, because contact with the dead made everyone there unclean. Memphis, near modern Cairo, was one of Egypt's great cities and a vast burial ground. A watchman was a lookout on a city wall who warned of danger.

In verse 7 Hosea quotes the insults thrown at him, fool and madman, and turns them back on his hearers. The days of Gibeah recall the outrage in Benjamin that led to civil war; some scholars think Hosea also has Saul's kingship, based at Gibeah, in mind.
passages.later: The Feast of Tabernacles was to be kept with joy after the harvest (Deuteronomy 16:13-15). Gibeah's crime and the war that followed fill the last chapters of Judges (Judges 19 to 21). Ezekiel too was made a watchman for Israel (Ezekiel 3:17).
passages.asks: Israel celebrated the harvest and forgot the God who sent it. Ask whether your joy in good things leads you to thank him or to forget him. And the prophet was called a fool for telling the truth. Ask whose warnings you have been quick to dismiss.

passages.t: Grapes in the wilderness, and a withered root
passages.happening:
God remembers the beginning. ‘I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the firstfruits of the fig tree in its first season’ (verse 10). But they went to Baal-peor and gave themselves to a shameful god, and became as detestable as the thing they loved.

Ephraim's glory will fly away like a bird (verse 11). The judgment falls on their children and their future (verses 11-13). The prophet breaks into a prayer that asks for childlessness (verse 14). All their evil is seen at Gilgal, and God will drive them from his house (verse 15). Ephraim is struck down, its root withered, and it cannot bear fruit (verse 16). ‘My God will reject them because they have not obeyed Him; and they shall be wanderers among the nations’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Here God himself looks back on Israel's history, starting with a tender memory. Grapes in the wilderness and the first figs of the season were rare delights. The contrast between that first delight and the present gives the chapter its grief.

Baal-peor recalls the time in the wilderness when Israelite men joined the worship of Baal of Peor with Moabite women, and a plague followed. People become like what they love. Gilgal, where Saul was made king, had become a center of corrupt worship.

In a world where children were the future of a family and the strength of a nation, the loss of children was the most terrible picture of judgment Hosea could use. Ephraim's name suggests fruitfulness, and the nation that sought children and harvests from Baal will lose its future. The last verse is the prophet's own solemn verdict: they will be wanderers among the nations.
passages.later: The sin at Baal-peor and the plague are told in Numbers 25:1-9. Saul was made king at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11:15). Jeremiah also remembered Israel's first love in the wilderness: ‘I remember the devotion of your youth’ (Jeremiah 2:2).
passages.hard:
How should the prayer for childlessness and the words about children in verses 11 to 16 be read?

These are among the most painful verses in the prophets, and readers rightly recoil. Several things help. The verses speak of a nation, not of particular mothers. The judgment is the reverse of what Israel sought from Baal, the fruit of womb and field, and having sought children from a fertility god, the nation will lose its future. The prayer in verse 14 seems to begin as a plea for the people and to break off in anguish, and many interpreters read Hosea as choosing, in a terrible situation, childlessness over the killing of children he foresaw in war (verse 13). And the words describe what invasion and siege would bring, as history confirmed.

None of this makes the passage easy. It must never be used to explain any family's loss, a miscarriage, a child who died, or a home without children, as God's punishment. When people asked Jesus whether a man was born blind because of someone's sin, he said it was neither his sin nor his parents' (John 9:3). The prophets speak of judgment on a nation under the covenant. They give no one a way to read a personal tragedy as a verdict.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God remembers finding Israel like grapes in the wilderness. Ask what it means to you that God remembers the beginning of your love for him. And Israel became like what it loved. Ask what your loves are making you into.
